title: Heralded Leakage Detection with Preserved Computational-State Coherence in a Fixed-Frequency Transmon
authors: Takeaki Miyamura, Zhiling Wang, Peter A. Spring, Hiroto Mukai, Kohei Matsuura, Jesper Ilves, Yoshiki Sunada, Yasunobu Nakamura
abstract: Leakage out of the computational subspace is a major error mechanism in superconducting quantum processors. Detecting leakage without disturbing the encoded quantum information can provide a heralded error signal that error-correction decoders exploit. However, standard dispersive readout collapses all qubit eigenstates indiscriminately. Here, we demonstrate heralded leakage detection on a fixed-frequency transmon by applying a Rabi drive on the computational transition during dispersive readout. The drive makes the computational states indistinguishable to the probe on the resonator while leaving the second and higher excited states distinguishable from the computational states. We achieve a leakage-detection fidelity of 97.1(3)% within the 80-ns detection window, with a false-flag rate of 2.3(3)% from the computational subspace. Conditioned on the no-leakage outcome, the post-detection state retains an average fidelity of 92.9(5)% across the six cardinal states for an equal mixture of computational and leakage population. The scheme requires no circuit elements beyond those used for standard dispersive readout, making it applicable to various types of superconducting qubits without hardware modification.
summary: The paper introduces a novel technique to detect leakage out of the computational subspace in transmon qubits during readout. By applying a specific Rabi drive, the authors make the desired computational states invisible to the measurement probe while allowing higher-energy leakage states to be detected. This method achieves high fidelity error flagging while minimizing back-action on the encoded quantum information.
main_problem: Leakage out of the computational subspace is a major error source in superconducting quantum processors, requiring detection without disturbing encoded quantum information.
main_result: The authors achieved a leakage-detection fidelity of 97.1% while preserving high coherence (92.9% average state fidelity) on the remaining computational states.
method: They apply a tailored Rabi drive during dispersive readout, which makes computational states indistinguishable to the probe while leaving higher excited leakage states distinguishable.
model_or_system: The system is a fixed-frequency transmon qubit coupled dispersively to a readout resonator (Circuit-QED). The analysis treats the system in at least a qutrit subspace ($\{|gangle, |eangle, |fangle\}$).
key_observables: Leakage-detection fidelity ($F_d$), false-flag rate ($\epsilon_{FF}$), post-detection average state fidelity ($ ar{F}$), and Rabi oscillation decay time ($T_{	ext{Rabi}}$).
important_parameters: Detection window (80 ns), qubit anharmonicity, drive detuning ($\delta$), and coupling strengths ($\chi$).
main_assumptions: The protocol requires no flux tunability or additional hardware components beyond standard dispersive readout elements.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the Rabi pulse sequence for characterization (measuring $T_{	ext{Rabi}}$) and the scheme itself, showing how the drive makes computational states invisible to the probe while leakage states remain visible.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical problem of measurement back-action, introduces the specific Rabi driving protocol to selectively couple/decouple subspaces, presents quantitative measurements of fidelity and coherence preservation, and discusses error decomposition.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses fundamental limitations in superconducting quantum hardware by providing a robust, non-invasive method for monitoring leakage errors, which is crucial for scaling up quantum computation.
